intro.title: Functional requirements
script: Let me start by agreeing on **what we're building**. Google Search is really two products glued together: a **web crawler** that downloads and understands a large fraction of the public web, and a **search engine** that answers a query against all of it in a fraction of a second.
I'll scope it to classic web search, ten blue links, because that's where the core architecture lives. Everything else Google shows on a results page sits on top of this.

cards.title: Crawl the web
lines: Discover and fetch billions of pages
script: First, we have to **crawl the web**. Nobody hands us a list of pages: we start from some seed URLs, download them, pull out the links, and follow those, over and over, until we've discovered **billions of pages** across hundreds of millions of sites.

cards.title: Keep it fresh
lines: News in minutes, popular pages daily,
the long tail every few weeks
script: Second, the web keeps changing, so crawling is never done. We need to **recrawl** pages at a rate that matches how fast they change and how much people care: a breaking news story should be searchable in **minutes**, a popular homepage daily, and some obscure forum thread from 2009 every few weeks.

cards.title: Index pages
lines: Parse HTML, extract text and links,
script: Third, we **index** what we crawl. We parse each page's HTML, pull out its text, title and links, and build an **inverted index**: for every word, the list of pages that contain it. That's the data structure that makes search possible at all.

cards.title: Keyword search
script: Fourth, the user-facing feature: someone types a **query**, and we return the **top ten results** out of the tens of billions of pages we know about.

cards.title: Ranking
script: Fifth, and this is what made Google win: **ranking**. Millions of pages may match a query; the order is the product. We'll combine **relevance**, how well the page's text matches the query, with **quality**, how trustworthy and important the page is, which we can learn from the link graph with something like **PageRank**.

cards.title: Results page
script: Sixth, each result on the page shows a **title, the URL, and a snippet**: a couple of sentences from the page with the query terms highlighted, so the user can judge the result without clicking it. That turns out to need its own storage.

cards.title: Autocomplete & spelling
script: And seventh, the query-side helpers: **autocomplete** suggestions as you type, and **spelling correction**, the "did you mean" line. Both are learned from what millions of other people searched for.

outOfScope.title: Out of scope
script: I'm leaving out **ads**, which is a whole auction system of its own, the **image, video, maps and news verticals**, **personalization**, the **knowledge graph** panels and AI answers, user accounts, and the details of **spam and abuse detection**.
I'll point at where some of these plug in, spam signals feed ranking for example, but I won't design them.
lines: Ads  ·  Images, video, maps & news verticals  ·  Personalization
Knowledge graph & AI answers  ·  Accounts  ·  Spam & abuse detection (details)

intro.title: Non-functional requirements
script: Now the qualities. This system has an unusual shape: a gigantic **offline pipeline** that can be slow and sloppy, feeding an **online service** that has to be extremely fast and never down. Most of the requirements land on one side or the other.

cards.title: Scale
script: **Scale**: we'll keep about **50 billion pages** in the index, out of many more we know exist. On the query side, roughly **8 to 9 billion searches a day**, so about **100,000 queries per second** on average and maybe **200,000** at peak.

cards.title: Latency
script: **Latency**: a search should take under **200 milliseconds at p99** on our side. Speed is a feature here; Google's own experiments found that a few hundred extra milliseconds measurably reduces how much people search. And because every query will touch many machines, it's the **tail** latency that will hurt us.

cards.title: Availability
script: **Availability**: serving needs **four nines** or better; Google being down is front-page news. The crawl and index pipeline is different: if it stalls for an hour, results get slightly staler and nobody notices. That asymmetry gives us a lot of freedom.

cards.title: Freshness
script: **Freshness**: important new pages, breaking news above all, should be searchable within **five minutes**. On average a page gets recrawled about every **ten days**, with a huge spread between hot and cold pages.

cards.title: Politeness
script: **Politeness** is a requirement you only get with crawlers. We must obey every site's **robots.txt**, and never hit one host hard enough to hurt it. Our crawler could take down a small site in seconds, and that's a fast way to get blocked everywhere.

cards.title: Consistency
script: **Consistency** is relaxed. Two users might briefly see slightly different results while a new index rolls out, and that's fine. There are no transactions here; the hard part is making each **query** see a coherent snapshot, not the whole system.

cards.title: Cost
script: And **cost**. The two big bills are the **machines serving the index**, which want it in RAM or flash for speed, and **crawl bandwidth and storage**. Every byte of posting list we shave off saves money on thousands of machines.

estimates.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimates
script: **50 billion pages** at ~**100 KB** each is about **5 PB** of HTML, a petabyte compressed. Recrawling every ten days means **5 billion fetches a day**: **60,000 pages a second**, about **50 Gbps**.

The compressed index is roughly **300 TB**, so about **1,000 shards**, each replicated. And the scary one: **200,000 queries a second** fanning out to **1,000 shards** is **200 million shard lookups a second**.

takeaway.title: Takeaway: two systems with opposite shapes
takeaway.heading: Takeaway: an offline pipeline feeding an online fan-out
script: So the takeaway: this is **two systems**. An **offline crawl and index pipeline**, measured in petabytes and pages per second, that optimizes for throughput and can tolerate delay and failure.

And an **online serving system** that has to scatter every query across about a thousand shards and gather the answers in under 200 milliseconds. There, **tail latency** is the enemy, because the query is only as fast as its slowest shard. The design is about keeping those two worlds apart and connecting them through one artifact: the **index**.
lines: Offline: 5 PB of pages, 60K fetches/s → throughput, batch jobs, tolerate lag
Online: 200K QPS × 1,000 shards in < 200 ms → scatter-gather, replicas, beat the tail

slides.title: Start with a toy search engine
script: Let's start with the **simplest search engine** that could possibly work: a user, and **one server**. The server keeps a list of pages and, in memory, a map from every word to the pages that contain it. A query comes in, we look up its words, intersect the lists, and send back the matches.
That's a perfectly good search engine for ten thousand pages. Every piece of the real system exists because this one box can't stretch to 50 billion pages and 200,000 queries a second.

slides.title: Get pages by crawling the web
script: Where do the pages come from? The server **crawls the web** itself: start from a few seed URLs, download each page, find the links in it, and add those to a to-do list. Repeat forever.

slides.title: Crawling and serving pull apart
script: Already there's a problem with keeping this in one box. **Crawling** is a throughput job: slow network calls, petabytes of data, and it's fine if it's a bit behind. **Serving** queries is a latency job: tiny requests that must be answered in milliseconds. Put them on the same machine and a big crawl batch makes searches slow. So the first move is to pull them apart.

slides.title: Split the crawler out
script: So the crawl moves to its own fleet of **fetchers**. A fetcher's job is narrow: take a URL, download it, hand the bytes on. It's almost all waiting on the network, so each machine runs **thousands of asynchronous connections** at once.

slides.title: Sizing the fetcher fleet
script: At 60,000 pages a second, and with a typical fetch taking a second or so end to end, we need tens of thousands of downloads in flight. A few hundred machines does it. And they're **stateless**: if one dies, its URLs just get handed out again.

items.detail: each fetch takes ~1 s end to end

items.text: **Tens of thousands** of downloads in flight

items.detail: a dead fetcher's URLs are handed out again

slides.title: The URL frontier
script: The fetchers need to know **what to download next**. That's the **URL frontier**, the crawler's to-do list. In the toy version it was a FIFO queue, which gives us a breadth-first crawl of the web.

slides.title: Two questions per batch
script: At our scale it isn't a simple queue, though. It has to answer two questions every time a fetcher asks for work: which URLs are **most important** to fetch now, and which ones can we fetch **without hammering any single site**. I'll come back to both in a moment; for now, the frontier hands out batches of URLs and the fetchers pull from it.

items.text: **Which hosts can we hit** without hammering them?

items.detail: fetchers pull work; the frontier never pushes

slides.title: Store every page we fetch
script: Fetched pages go into a **page store**: petabytes keyed by URL, with a few timestamped **versions per page**. A wide-column store like **Bigtable** fits well, and keying rows by **reversed hostname**, com.example.www/path, keeps each site's pages together for fast scans.
Keeping the raw HTML, not just what we extract from it, means we can **re-parse and re-index** the whole web when the parser improves, without crawling it again.

slides.title: Parse pages into text and links
script: Next, a **parser** turns raw HTML into something useful. It extracts the **title, the visible text, and the outgoing links**, along with the anchor text of each link. It detects the language, normalizes character sets, and strips boilerplate like navigation menus.

Parsing is CPU-heavy and completely independent per page, so it's an easy batch or streaming job that scales out on as many machines as we like. Its outputs feed two places: the **links** go back to the crawler, and the **text** goes on to indexing.

slides.title: Don't crawl the same URL twice
script: Every page has dozens of links, and most point to pages we already know about. So before anything goes back into the frontier we check a **URL DB**: every URL we've ever seen, plus its crawl history, when we last fetched it, whether it changed, and its links.

First, we **normalize** URLs: lowercase the host, drop default ports, sort query parameters, strip tracking junk like session IDs. Then the check is a lookup by a hash of the normalized URL. With hundreds of billions of known URLs, it's a big sharded key-value table, and a **Bloom filter** in front of it answers "definitely new" for most links without touching disk.

slides.title: A scheduler closes the crawl loop
script: Now the loop closes with a **recrawl scheduler**. It reads the URL DB and decides **what to fetch next, and when**. New URLs get a priority based on how important their linking pages are. Known URLs get a next-fetch time based on how often they've changed in the past and how much people care about them.

slides.title: Adaptive recrawl intervals
script: This is where the freshness requirement lives. A news homepage that changes every few minutes gets fetched every few minutes; a page that hasn't changed in a year drifts to the back. If a fetch shows a page didn't change, we stretch its interval; if it did change, we shrink it. The scheduler pushes due URLs into the frontier, and the cycle runs forever.

steps.note: unchanged → stretch the interval · changed → shrink it

slides.title: Politeness: robots.txt and rate limits
script: Now **politeness**. Before fetching from a host, we check its **robots.txt**, which says which paths crawlers may visit. We fetch it once per host, keep it in a **robots cache** for a day or so, and check every URL against it.

slides.title: Inside the frontier: front queues
script: Rate limiting lives in the frontier, so let's zoom in. Its first layer is **front queues by priority**: the scheduler drops each URL into the queue that matches its importance, and the most important queue is drained most often.

slides.title: Back queues: one per host
script: The second layer is **back queues by host**. Each back queue holds one host's URLs and enforces a minimum delay between requests, so a big site is crawled one connection at a time while thousands of others run in parallel. Slow or erroring hosts get longer delays.

slides.title: Cache DNS lookups
script: A less obvious bottleneck: **DNS**. Every fetch needs the host's IP address, and public resolvers are slow and rate-limited. At 60,000 fetches a second, DNS would quickly become the crawler's slowest step.

slides.title: One lookup, many fetches
script: So we run our own **DNS cache** for the crawler. Because back queues already group URLs by host, one lookup usually serves many fetches. It's a small component, but it's the kind of thing that decides whether a crawler reaches its throughput target.

steps.note: next URL from the same host's back queue

slides.title: Duplicates and crawler traps
script: Two problems for the parser and URL DB. First, **duplicate content**: maybe a third of the web is copies and mirrors. Exact copies are a content hash; for near-duplicates a **SimHash** fingerprint differs by only a few bits when pages differ by an ad or a date. We index one canonical page per cluster.

slides.title: Escaping crawler traps
script: Second, **crawler traps**, like a calendar with "next month" forever. We cap depth and URLs per host, spot repeating path patterns, and give each site a **crawl budget** based on how valuable its pages are.

items.detail: scaled by how valuable its pages are

slides.title: Build an inverted index
script: With clean documents coming out of the parser, we build the **inverted index**: for every term, a **posting list** of the documents containing it, with positions and fields, so we can match phrases and tell a title hit from a footer hit.

It's a classic **MapReduce**: emit (term, docID, positions), shuffle by term, reduce into sorted, **delta-compressed** posting lists. That's how 5 PB of HTML becomes a few hundred TB of index, which the server now queries. But that's far too big for one machine.

slides.title: Shard the index by document
script: Three hundred terabytes means about **1,000 shards**. The question is how to split the index, and there are two classic ways.

slides.title: Partition by term or by document
script: **Term partitioning** gives each shard some of the words. A query touches few shards, but "cat AND dog" ships huge posting lists between machines, and popular words become hot spots.

**Document partitioning** gives each shard a slice of the **documents**, with a complete index for them. Every query hits **every shard**, but each returns only its local **top few results**, so little crosses the network and load is even. That's what we'll use, with every shard **replicated** for availability and throughput.

rows: huge posting lists cross the network; hot words
fan-out, but each shard returns only its top few

slides.title: A search service and a root mixer
script: The single server now splits in two. A **search service** owns the user's request: it parses the query, calls the backends, and builds the results page. Behind it, a **root mixer** does the distributed part: it sends the query to a replica of every shard, waits for their answers, and **merges** the per-shard top results into one global list.

slides.title: Why two services
script: Separating them keeps the fan-out logic in one place. Product features, layout and experiments change constantly in the search service. The root mixer is a tight, performance-critical piece of infrastructure that changes rarely.

rows: the user's request, the results page

slides.title: Scatter-gather and the tail
script: The fan-out's weak spot: a query is only as fast as its **slowest shard**. If each shard is slow one time in a hundred, a query touching a thousand is slow **almost every time**.

slides.title: Taming the tail
script: Defenses: **intermediate aggregators**, so the root talks to ~30 mixers of ~30 shards each instead of a thousand machines. **Hedged requests**: if a shard is slower than its usual p95, ask another replica and take the first answer. And **partial results**: past the deadline, answer without the straggler. Losing one shard in a thousand costs a little recall nobody notices; a slow page, everybody notices.

items.detail: slower than its p95? ask another replica, take the first
past the deadline, answer without the straggler

slides.title: PageRank: quality from the link graph
script: Matching text alone ranks badly: the pages with the most copies of a word are usually spam. We need a sense of **quality**, and the web gives us a great signal for it: **links**. A link is a vote, and a vote from an important page counts more.

That's **PageRank**: a page's score is the sum of its linkers' scores, each divided by their out-link count, iterated over the **link graph** in a batch job until it settles. The result is a **static quality score** per page that the indexer stores, so shards can order posting lists best-first.

slides.title: Rank in two phases
script: Ranking every match carefully is impossible: a common query matches millions of pages. So ranking happens in **two phases**.

slides.title: Phase one on every shard
script: In the first, each shard uses a **cheap score**, text match like BM25 combined with the static quality score, to pick its local best handful of candidates. That's fast because posting lists are already ordered by quality, so a shard can often stop early.

steps.note: posting lists are best-first, so stop early

slides.title: Phase two: the ML re-ranker
script: In the second phase, the root sends the merged top **thousand or so** candidates to an **ML re-ranker**. Here we can afford hundreds of features per document: where the terms appear, how close together, anchor text, freshness, the language and location match, spam scores, and how users interacted with this result before. A learned model turns those into the final order of the top ten.

slides.title: Doc servers for titles and snippets
script: Once we know the top ten document IDs, we need what's actually shown: the **title, URL and snippet**. Snippets are **query-dependent**: we pick the sentences from the page that best match this particular query, and highlight the words. So we can't precompute them.

slides.title: Fetching snippets for the top ten
script: That's the job of the **doc servers**: a second sharded store, partitioned by document ID, holding a compressed copy of each page's text. The root asks only the doc servers holding those ten documents, so it's a small, targeted lookup, unlike the full fan-out to the index. The indexer builds these alongside the index shards.

steps.note: fan-out, merge and re-rank → top 10 doc IDs
only the servers holding the top 10, not a full fan-out

slides.title: A front end in every datacenter
script: Now the front door. Users reach a **front end** layer, Google calls it the GFE. DNS and anycast send each user to a nearby datacenter, and the front end ends **TLS**, protects against abuse, and **load-balances** across a pool of stateless search service machines.
Since the search service holds no state, we scale it by adding machines and route around failed ones with health checks. The interesting state, the index, lives further back.

slides.title: Cache whole result pages
script: Query traffic is very skewed: a big chunk of searches repeat ones made in the last few minutes, think of a celebrity's name or a sports score. So before fanning out to a thousand shards, the search service checks a **results cache** keyed by the normalized query plus language and region.

A hit skips the whole backend, which is the cheapest way to cut load. Entries live for minutes, not days, so results stay fresh, and they're **invalidated** when a new index version rolls out. With hit rates around **30%**, that's a third of a very expensive fan-out avoided.

slides.title: Rewrite the query first
script: What users type is often not the best thing to search for. A **query rewriter** runs before the fan-out.

slides.title: What the rewriter does
script: It fixes **spelling**, "recieve" to "receive", using a model built from billions of past queries and their corrections. It adds **synonyms** and word variants, so "running shoes" also matches "run" and "sneakers". And it notices things like a place or language in the query.

This one step adds a lot of recall: the best page for a misspelled query usually doesn't contain the misspelling. When the correction is confident we search for it directly; otherwise we show "did you mean".

slides.title: A streaming path for fresh pages
script: Now the freshness problem. Rebuilding a 300-terabyte index with MapReduce takes hours, and rolling it out takes longer. That's fine for most of the web, but not for a news story that broke five minutes ago. So we add a second, **streaming** path.

slides.title: Batch and streaming indexing
script: When the scheduler marks a page as hot, a news site or something trending, the parser also sends it to a **fresh indexer**, which indexes documents one at a time as they arrive. This is roughly the move Google made from batch indexing to its incremental **Caffeine** system: process each document as it's crawled instead of waiting for the next big rebuild.

slides.title: Query a fresh tier and the base index
script: The fresh indexer writes into a small **fresh index**: just the last few hours of hot pages, small enough to keep entirely in memory and update within **seconds**.

The root mixer now queries **both tiers**: the big base index and the fresh index, and merges them, preferring the fresh copy when a document appears in both. When the next base build includes those pages, they age out of the fresh tier. This **tiered index** gives us minutes-level freshness for the pages that need it without paying for streaming updates across all 50 billion.

slides.title: Trace one search end to end
script: Let's trace one query through what we've built. The user's request lands on the nearest **front end**, which picks a **search service** machine. It checks the **results cache**; on a miss, the **query rewriter** fixes and expands the query.

slides.title: Scatter, rank, and render
script: The **root mixer** scatters it to every **index shard** and the **fresh index**, merges their top candidates, has the **ML re-ranker** order the best thousand, and fetches **snippets** for the top ten. The search service renders the page and caches it. Fan-out and re-ranking take about **100 ms** of the budget.

slides.title: Log every query and click
script: Every search, and every click on a result, gets written asynchronously to **query logs**, a durable stream that batch jobs read later. Logging is fire-and-forget, so it never slows the search down.

These logs turn out to be one of the most valuable datasets in the system. They tell us what people **search for**, what they **misspell**, and which results they actually **chose**. The next few pieces all learn from them.

slides.title: Autocomplete from popular queries
script: **Autocomplete** has to answer on every keystroke, so its latency budget is even tighter than search: tens of milliseconds. It can't fan out to the index; instead it has its own **prefix index**, built offline from the query logs.

Think of a **trie** of popular queries where each node already stores the **top-K completions** for that prefix, so a lookup is just walking down a few characters. It's rebuilt from the logs regularly, with a fast lane for queries that are trending right now. We also filter out offensive or very rare queries, so we never suggest something only one person ever typed.

slides.title: Train ranking on clicks
script: The logs also feed **ranking**. When users consistently skip result three and click result five, that's a signal the order is wrong. Click data, with care for position bias since people click the top results more no matter what, becomes **training data** for the re-ranker, along with ratings from human evaluators.

Models are retrained offline and rolled out behind **experiments**: a small slice of traffic gets the new model, and we compare engagement before shipping it to everyone. Spelling correction learns the same way, from users who retype a query a moment later.

slides.title: Roll out a new index safely
script: One more detail on the boundary between the offline and online worlds: how a freshly built index gets to the shards. We never update a serving shard in place. The indexer writes a complete new **immutable** version of each shard, the shard servers copy it in the background, and then swap to it.

slides.title: Replica by replica
script: We roll that out **replica by replica**, so most replicas keep serving while some swap, and we check result quality on the new version before going further. If something looks wrong, we **roll back** to the previous version, which is still on disk. During the rollout, different replicas serve different versions, which is exactly the eventual consistency we agreed was acceptable.

steps.note: B keeps serving v41 while A swaps
looks wrong? roll back to v41, still on disk

slides.title: Replicate across datacenters
script: Finally, **availability at Google scale**. The whole serving stack, front ends, search services, index shards, doc servers, caches, is replicated in **many datacenters** around the world, each holding a full copy of the index. Users go to the nearest one, which also saves latency.

slides.title: Read-only serving makes failover easy
script: If a datacenter fails or needs maintenance, the front end layer and DNS route its traffic to others. Since serving is read-only and the index is just copied out, replicating it is easy; there's no cross-region write coordination to worry about. The crawl and index pipeline doesn't need this: it can run in a few big datacenters and ship finished indexes everywhere.

items.text: **Failover**: DNS and front ends route around

items.detail: the index is just copied out; no cross-region writes

slides.title: The complete system
script: So here's the whole design. At the bottom, the **offline pipeline**: a polite, prioritized crawl loop feeding a batch indexer and PageRank, plus a streaming fresh indexer for what's hot. It optimizes for **throughput** and can lag. At the top, the **online system**: a root mixer scattering each query over ~1,000 **document-partitioned, replicated shards**, re-ranking with ML, in under 200 ms.
They meet at one artifact, the **immutable index**, and query logs close the loop for ranking, spelling and autocomplete. With more time, I'd go deeper on the ranking model and spam.
